subject: english-literature
title: Whose Voice Speaks?
welcome_lead: Every novel is filtered through a voice. First-person, third-person, omniscient or limited — identify the lens.
meta_desc: Narrative voice in prose — first, third, omniscient, limited and unreliable at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You can now diagnose narrative voice — the most powerful prose technique a writer wields.

concepts.def: The narrator is a character within the story (I went.), offering immediacy and bias.
Narrator stands outside the story with access to all characters' thoughts and events.
Narrator stands outside but restricts knowledge to one character's perspective.
Wayne Booth (1961) — narrator whose account the reader is invited to distrust.
Rare 'you' narration (Bright Lights, Big City) that implicates the reader.
Texts using several first-person voices (The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying).

walkthroughs.body_html:
First-person narration grants intimate access to one consciousness. Jane Eyre, Pip in Great Expectations and Nick Carraway in Gatsby each filter events through their own moral lens.

The reader's challenge is to discern where the narrator may be wrong, partial or self-deceived.
Third-person omniscient narration can swoop into any consciousness. Tolstoy moves between Pierre, Natasha and Andrei in War and Peace; Eliot anatomises a whole town in Middlemarch.

Wayne Booth coined unreliable narrator in The Rhetoric of Fiction (1961). The narrator's values diverge from the implied author's.

Stevens in The Remains of the Day is unreliable: the reader senses his self-deception through what he carefully avoids saying.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
An unreliable narrator is when the author makes mistakes.
The speaker is whoever reads the poem out loud.
An unreliable narrator is when the author makes mistakes.
An unreliable narrator is one who tells lies in the story.
Their account is undermined within the text by ignorance, bias, self-deception or deceit, so the reader must read against what they say.
